title: Soda Bread
subtitle: Irish brown soda bread ready in under an hour
excerpt: Wholemeal and white flour combined with buttermilk and bicarbonate of soda, formed into a round, scored with a cross, and baked for 35 minutes. No yeast, no proving time. Crusty outside, soft and slightly dense inside.

recipe.sourceNotes: Soda bread became the everyday bread of Ireland in the 1840s when bicarbonate of soda became widely available at the same time that the potato famine made conventional grains scarce. The acid in buttermilk reacts with the bicarbonate of soda to produce carbon dioxide, which leavens the bread without yeast. Traditional Irish soda bread uses only wholemeal flour; the brown and white blend is a common modern variation. The cross scored on top is traditional and has two functions: it helps the bread bake through and, by folklore, it blesses the bread.

content.text: Handle the dough as little as possible: overworking makes a tough loaf. The dough should be soft and slightly sticky but hold its shape when patted into a round. It should go straight into the oven once mixed: unlike yeast breads, there is no benefit to resting. The loaf is done when it sounds hollow when tapped on the base.
Heat the oven to 200 C / fan 180 C / gas 6. Line a baking tray with baking paper.
Mix both flours, bicarbonate of soda, and salt in a large bowl. Make a well in the centre. Pour in the buttermilk. Mix quickly with a fork until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork.

Turn out onto a lightly floured surface. Shape quickly into a round about 18 cm in diameter. Place on the lined tray. Cut a deep cross in the top, almost to the base. Brush with melted butter if using.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the crust is golden and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the base. Cool on a rack for at least 15 minutes before cutting. Best eaten the day it is made.
